mcq.q: NLP provides computers with the capability of understanding text and spoken words:

opts.t: in the same way a human being can understand, interpret and generate human language
faster than a human being can

mcq.exp: The definition's key phrase is "in the same way a human being can".

mcq.q: How many levels of linguistic knowledge does the course list?
mcq.exp: Six: phonetics/phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, discourse.

mcq.q: Knowledge about linguistic sounds is:
mcq.exp: Phonetics and Phonology.

mcq.q: Knowledge of the meaningful components of words is:
mcq.exp: Morphology — morphemes are the meaningful components.

mcq.q: Knowledge of the structural relationships between words is:
mcq.exp: Syntax.

mcq.q: Knowledge of the relationship of meaning to the goals and intentions of the speaker is:
mcq.exp: Pragmatics — the word "intentions" is the giveaway.

mcq.q: Knowledge about linguistic units larger than a single utterance is:
mcq.exp: Discourse.

mcq.q: The word "unsweetened" is used in the deck to illustrate:
mcq.exp: Morphology — un + sweet + ened.

mcq.q: How many distinct units of meaning does "unsweetened" break into?
mcq.exp: Three: un- (prefix), sweet (root), -ened (suffix).

mcq.q: "Latte iced get an I milk oat with can?" is ungrammatical, which demonstrates that:

opts.t: syntax governs word order and sentence structure

mcq.exp: Both sentences contain the same words, so only word order distinguishes them — that is syntax.

mcq.q: Taking "I'm freezing" to literally mean body temperature has dropped to 0 °C is an example of:
mcq.exp: Semantics deals purely with dictionary definitions.

mcq.q: Saying "I'm freezing" to a barista near an open door to mean "please close the door" is an example of:
mcq.exp: Pragmatics — same sentence, but now the speaker's intent.

mcq.q: Turn-taking, context references and conversational flow belong to:
mcq.exp: Discourse.

mcq.q: The difference between the /p/ in "please" and the /p/ in "cup" is:

opts.t: aspiration — a puff of air on "please" but not at the end of "cup"

mcq.exp: Aspiration — a puff of air on "please", none at the end of "cup".

mcq.q: Which statement correctly separates phonetics from phonology?

opts.t: Phonetics deals with physical production; phonology deals with how the brain categorizes sounds into meaningful patterns
Phonetics categorizes sounds; phonology produces them

mcq.exp: Phonetics = physical production; phonology = brain-level categorization.

mcq.q: In the HAL example, "can't" as a contraction of can + not illustrates:
mcq.exp: A contraction is a morpheme combination — morphology.

mcq.q: In the HAL example, HAL politely refusing rather than being physically unable illustrates:
mcq.exp: Pragmatics — the hidden intent behind "can't".

mcq.q: In the HAL example, the subordinate clause [I'm afraid] introducing an embedded main clause [I can't do that] illustrates:
mcq.exp: Clause structure is syntax.

mcq.q: "What year was Abraham Lincoln born?" can be answered by:
mcq.exp: A single dated fact — a simple search engine suffices.

mcq.q: "What do scientists think about the ethics of human cloning?" requires:

opts.t: synthesizing and summarizing information from multiple sources
drawing conclusions from a single known fact

mcq.exp: An opinion spread across many sources — requires synthesis and summarization.

mcq.q: Ambiguity is defined as:

opts.t: multiple alternative linguistic structures for the same input

mcq.exp: Multiple alternative linguistic structures.

mcq.q: Most tasks in speech and language processing can be viewed as:
mcq.exp: Resolving ambiguity.

mcq.q: In "I saw the waiter with glasses", the reading where "with glasses" attaches to the verb "saw" is:
mcq.exp: Attachment of a prepositional phrase is a structural (syntactic) choice.

mcq.q: The reading "a waiter carrying serving tumblers" is an example of:
mcq.exp: The word "glasses" itself has two senses — lexical/semantic.

mcq.q: The reading "the waiter was in the physical company of drinking glasses" is:
mcq.exp: Pragmatic — grammatically valid but an odd image.

mcq.q: How many readings of "I made her duck" does the deck give?
mcq.exp: Five.

mcq.q: Deciding whether "duck" is a verb or a noun is solved by:
mcq.exp: Verb vs noun is exactly what POS tagging decides.

mcq.q: Deciding whether "make" means "create" or "cook" is solved by:
mcq.exp: Two senses of one word — word sense disambiguation.

mcq.q: The two important kinds of lexical disambiguation are:
mcq.exp: Part-of-speech and word sense.

mcq.q: A text-to-speech system reading "lead" must decide between "lead pipe" and "lead me on". This is an instance of:
mcq.exp: Two pronunciations of one spelling, resolved lexically.

mcq.q: The single biggest hurdle in NLP, per the deck, is:
mcq.exp: "Ambiguity is the single biggest hurdle in NLP."

mcq.q: Why do machines struggle with ambiguity where humans do not?

opts.t: humans resolve it instantly using world knowledge, while the same input can build multiple alternative parse trees for a machine

mcq.exp: World knowledge vs multiple parse trees.

mcq.q: Zipf's Law states:
mcq.exp: Frequency α 1/Rank — inverse, not direct.

mcq.q: The "Long Tail" problem means:

opts.t: rare occurrences collectively matter but are hard to train
sentences are too long to parse

mcq.exp: Rare occurrences collectively matter but are hard to train.

mcq.q: Under Zipf's law, machines receive mountains of data for:

opts.t: common words like is, a, the

mcq.exp: Common function words; rare words are the problem.

mcq.q: In "Rose rose to put rose roes on her rows of roses", the token "roes" means:
mcq.exp: roe = fish eggs / caviar. "rows" is the one meaning organized lines.

mcq.q: In the same sentence, the second "rose" is:

opts.t: a past-tense verb meaning stood up

mcq.exp: Past tense of rise.

mcq.q: In "Will will will will's will?", the final "will" is:

opts.t: the legal document stating who gets his possessions
the verb meaning to pass on

mcq.exp: The legal document — a noun.

mcq.q: Without which three things does a computer struggle with these tongue-twister sentences?
mcq.exp: Capitalization, context and part-of-speech tags.

mcq.q: Which sentence is NOT one of the ambiguity examples in the deck?

opts.t: I saw the waiter with glasses

mcq.exp: "The old man the boat" is a real garden-path sentence but is not in this deck.

mcq.q: Evaluating customer reviews to determine tone is:
mcq.exp: Sentiment Analysis & Opinion Mining.

mcq.q: Discovering latent abstract themes across large document collections without human labeling is:
mcq.exp: Topic Modeling — the phrase "without human labeling" distinguishes it from Text Classification.

mcq.q: Understanding that "how to fix a flat" refers to a tire is an example of:

opts.t: semantic search interpreting user intent and context

mcq.exp: Semantic search moves beyond keyword matching.

mcq.q: Extractive summarization:

opts.t: pulls the most important sentences directly from the document

mcq.exp: Extractive pulls existing sentences.

mcq.q: Abstractive summarization:
mcq.exp: Abstractive generates new text.

mcq.q: Converting acoustic speech signals into written text is:
mcq.exp: Automatic Speech Recognition.

mcq.q: Identifying or authenticating speakers from the unique phonetic characteristics of their voice is:
mcq.exp: Voice Biometrics.

mcq.q: "Book a table for two at 8 PM." → ReserveRestaurant is an example of:
mcq.exp: Intent Recognition — it identifies the user's goal.

mcq.q: Classifying a message as spam or ham is:
mcq.exp: Spam Detection; spam vs ham is its defining vocabulary.

mcq.q: "Bonjour tout le monde" → French is:
mcq.exp: Language Detection.

mcq.q: Extracting amounts, dates and vendor names from unstructured documents is:
mcq.exp: Invoice Parsing.

mcq.q: "Elon Musk founded Tesla in Austin, Texas." → PERSON, ORG, LOC tags is:
mcq.exp: NER tags proper nouns by type.

mcq.q: "Marie Curie discovered Radium." → (Marie Curie)–[discovered]→(Radium) is:
mcq.exp: Relation Mining links two entities.

mcq.q: Extracting "Type 2 diabetes" and "500mg of Metformin" from a patient record is:
mcq.exp: Medical NER — clinical entities, medications, dosages.

mcq.q: Detecting an incident and capturing its participants, time and location is:
mcq.exp: Event Extraction.

mcq.q: "The cat chased the mouse." → "The mouse was chased by the cat." is:
mcq.exp: Paraphrasing — same meaning, different wording.

mcq.q: In the NLP pipeline, Step 1 "Problem Definition & Context" maps to:
mcq.exp: Unit 1 — Background & NLP-Hard.

mcq.q: Pipeline Step 4, "Linguistic Feature Extraction", maps to:
mcq.exp: Unit 5 — note the pipeline and unit numbers cross over here.

mcq.q: Pipeline Step 5, "Language Modeling & Stats", maps to:
mcq.exp: Unit 4 — the other half of the crossover.

mcq.q: Pipeline Step 3, "Data Preprocessing & Cleaning", maps to:
mcq.exp: Unit 3.

mcq.q: Which unit covers Semantics, Pragmatics and Discourse?
mcq.exp: Unit 6.

mcq.q: Which industries does the deck say NLP applications spread across?
mcq.exp: Healthcare, Finance, Commerce, Legal.

mcq.q: The four stages of speech production, in order, are:
mcq.exp: Breathing → Phonation → Resonance → Articulation.

mcq.q: In speech production, airflow serves as the source during:
mcq.exp: Breathing.

mcq.q: The action of the vocal folds in the larynx is:
mcq.exp: Phonation.

mcq.q: The pharynx, oral and nasal cavity amplifying sound is:
mcq.exp: Resonance.

mcq.q: The tongue, lips, teeth, palate and jaw shaping the airstream is:
mcq.exp: Articulation.

mcq.q: Voiced sounds are made with:

opts.t: the vocal folds together and vibrating
the vocal folds apart and still

mcq.exp: Vocal folds together and vibrating.

mcq.q: Which group is entirely voiced?
mcq.exp: Note that all English vowels are voiced.

mcq.q: Nasal sounds use:

opts.t: both the oral and nasal tracts as resonating cavities

mcq.exp: Both tracts act as resonating cavities.

mcq.q: English nasal sounds are:
mcq.exp: m, n, ng.

mcq.q: Consonants are made by:

opts.t: restricting or blocking the airflow in some way

mcq.exp: Restricting or blocking airflow; they may be voiced or unvoiced.

mcq.q: Compared with consonants, vowels are:

opts.t: generally louder and longer-lasting, with less obstruction, and usually voiced

mcq.exp: Less obstruction, usually voiced, louder and longer.

mcq.q: Semivowels are:

opts.t: voiced like vowels but short and less syllabic like consonants

mcq.exp: Properties of both categories.

mcq.q: The semivowels given are:
mcq.exp: [y] and [w]. ([r] and [l] are approximants, not semivowels, in this deck.)

mcq.q: Place of articulation refers to:
mcq.exp: Place = WHERE = point of maximum restriction.

mcq.q: Manner of articulation refers to:
mcq.exp: Manner = HOW the restriction is made.

mcq.q: A consonant that completely blocks airflow during closure, followed by an explosive release, is a:
mcq.exp: Stop / plosive — complete closure then explosive release.

mcq.q: Sounds that constrict airflow to create turbulent "hissing" are:
mcq.exp: Fricatives.

mcq.q: Affricates combine:
mcq.exp: Stop + fricative.

mcq.q: [ch] as in "chicken" and [jh] as in "giraffe" are:
mcq.exp: Affricates.

mcq.q: The higher-pitched fricatives [s], [z], [sh] and [zh] are called:
mcq.exp: Sibilants.

mcq.q: Approximants are produced with articulators:

opts.t: close together but not narrow enough to create turbulent airflow

mcq.exp: Close, but not enough to make turbulence — that is what separates them from fricatives.

mcq.q: [l] is described as a lateral sound because:

opts.t: the tongue tip is at the alveolar ridge with the sides lowered to allow airflow
it is produced at the side of the face

mcq.exp: Sides lowered to allow airflow = lateral.

mcq.q: Which pair correctly contrasts a fricative with an approximant?
mcq.exp: /v/ fricative vs /w/ approximant — Van/Wan, Vest/West, Vine/Wine.

mcq.q: A quick single strike of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, heard in the middle of "lotus" in American English, is a:
mcq.exp: Tap or flap [dx]; many UK dialects use [t] there instead.

mcq.q: Vowels are classified based on:
mcq.exp: Tongue position and height.

mcq.q: A vowel in which the tongue position changes markedly during production is a:
mcq.exp: Diphthong.

mcq.q: IPA is:

opts.t: a universal system designed to transcribe all spoken human languages accurately

mcq.exp: IPA is universal.

mcq.q: ARPAbet is designed specifically to represent:

opts.t: American English phonemes in ASCII text

mcq.exp: ARPAbet is American English in ASCII.

mcq.q: In ARPAbet, the digit 1 attached to a vowel code means:
mcq.exp: 1 = primary stress.

mcq.q: In ARPAbet, the digit 0 means:
mcq.exp: 0 = unstressed.

mcq.q: How does IPA mark stress?

opts.t: diacritic tick marks before stressed syllables

mcq.exp: Diacritic tick marks before the stressed syllable, e.g. /ˈkæt/.

mcq.q: Which is an ARPAbet symbol rather than IPA?
mcq.exp: EH1 is ASCII with a stress digit — ARPAbet. The others are IPA symbols.

mcq.q: The vowel core of a syllable is called the:
mcq.exp: Nucleus.

mcq.q: The initial consonant or set of consonants of a syllable is the:
mcq.exp: Onset.

mcq.q: The set of consonants following the nucleus is the:
mcq.exp: Coda.

mcq.q: The rime (or rhyme) is:
mcq.exp: Nucleus + coda — the onset is never included.

mcq.q: "stop" (/stɑːp/) has which syllabic form?
mcq.exp: CCVC — /st/ onset, /ɑː/ nucleus, /p/ coda.

mcq.q: "milk" (/mɪlk/) has which syllabic form?
mcq.exp: CVCC — /m/ onset, /ɪ/ nucleus, /lk/ coda.

mcq.q: "plant" (/plænt/) has which syllabic form?
mcq.exp: CCVCC — /pl/ onset, /æ/ nucleus, /nt/ coda.

mcq.q: In the word "new" (/njuː/), the coda is:

opts.t: empty — it is an open syllable

mcq.exp: Empty coda → an open syllable → no rime.

mcq.q: In "eggs" (/ɛɡz/), the onset is:

opts.t: empty — the syllable starts with a vowel

mcq.exp: Empty onset — the syllable starts on the vowel.

mcq.q: In "green" (/ɡriːn/), the rime is:
mcq.exp: Rime = nucleus /iː/ + coda /n/ = /iːn/.

mcq.q: Prosody covers properties that extend over:
mcq.exp: Whole syllables, words or sentences — not individual phonemes.

mcq.q: "You're coming." with falling pitch vs "You're coming?" with rising pitch demonstrates:
mcq.exp: Intonation — sentence-level pitch contour.

mcq.q: "CONduct" (noun) vs "conDUCT" (verb) demonstrates:
mcq.exp: Lexical stress — it changes the part of speech.

mcq.q: Syllables which are more prominent are called:
mcq.exp: Accented syllables.

mcq.q: "Woman, without her man, is nothing." vs "Woman: without her, man is nothing." illustrates:
mcq.exp: Prosodic boundaries / phrasing.

mcq.q: Which acoustic parameter of prosody comes from air pressure from the lungs?
mcq.exp: Intensity/amplitude comes from lung air pressure; pitch comes from vocal fold vibration rate.

mcq.q: Fundamental frequency corresponds to:
mcq.exp: Rate of vocal fold vibration.

mcq.q: The function of duration in prosody is:

opts.t: marking pauses, syllable elongation and overall tempo

mcq.exp: Pauses, elongation and tempo.

mcq.q: The sampling relationship given in the deck is:
mcq.exp: fₛ = 1/T.

mcq.q: The spectrogram magnitude is written as:
In |X(m,k)|, the magnitude is evaluated at:
mcq.exp: ω = 2πk/N.

mcq.q: Frequency-domain analysis in the course begins with:
mcq.exp: Fourier series, leading to the DFT spectrum and then the spectrogram.

mcq.q: Sequence labelling is the task of assigning:

opts.t: a categorical label to each item in a continuous sequence of input data
a numeric score to a sentence
a parse tree to a sentence
a single label to a whole document

mcq.exp: A label per item in a continuous sequence — that is what makes it a sequence task.

mcq.q: Voice activity detection is given as an example of:
mcq.exp: VAD labels each frame speech / non-speech.

mcq.q: Sequence labelling spans inputs ranging from:

opts.t: raw acoustic signals to textual and semantic units

mcq.exp: From raw acoustic signals to textual and semantic units.

mcq.q: A language is defined in the deck as:

opts.t: a collection of valid strings built from a set of characters

mcq.exp: A collection of valid strings built from a set of characters.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the four raw-text noise sources listed?
mcq.exp: The four listed are HTML formatting, emojis, informal spellings and inconsistent casing.

mcq.q: Misreading "rn" as "m" is which OCR error class?
mcq.exp: Visually similar characters — 0/O, 1/I/l, cl/d, rn/m.

mcq.q: "I n f o r m a t i o n" with spaces between every letter is:
mcq.exp: Hyper-segmentation is a word boundary error.

mcq.q: Multi-column text being read straight across is:
mcq.exp: Layout breakdown.

mcq.q: Dust and paper creases becoming mis-punctuation is:
mcq.exp: Scan artifacts.

mcq.q: The pattern /[wW]/ matches:
mcq.exp: Square brackets are a disjunction of characters.

mcq.q: The pattern /[^a]/ matches:

opts.t: the start of a line then a

mcq.exp: Caret first inside brackets = negation.

mcq.q: Which operator means "the preceding character or nothing"?
mcq.exp: The question mark. Square brackets cannot express "s or nothing".

mcq.q: /aa*/ matches:
mcq.exp: One mandatory a, then zero or more ⇒ one or more.

mcq.q: Why is the RE for an integer /[0-9][0-9]*/ rather than /[0-9]*/?

opts.t: because /[0-9]*/ also matches the empty string

mcq.exp: * means zero or more, so /[0-9]*/ matches "" as well as "5" and "123".

opts.t: any digit repeated at least four times
any digit repeated exactly four times

mcq.exp: Curly brackets give an exact repetition count.

mcq.q: Are /baaa*!/ and /baa+!/ the same?

opts.t: Yes, both represent a minimum of 2 a's

mcq.exp: Yes — both require a minimum of 2 a's.

mcq.q: The period /./ matches:
mcq.exp: Any single character except newline; \. escapes it.

mcq.q: /nlp.*nlp/ is used to:

opts.t: match a line where nlp appears twice
match nlp at the start of a line

mcq.exp: /.*/ finds any line where the word appears twice.

mcq.q: Which are the three uses of the caret ^?

opts.t: start of line, negation inside brackets, and just a caret
end of line, grouping, and repetition

mcq.exp: Start of line, negation inside brackets, and a literal caret.

mcq.q: In "The cat in the cathedral was scattered", /\bcat\b/ matches:
mcq.exp: \b requires word boundaries on both sides — only the standalone "cat".

mcq.q: In the same sentence, /\Bcat\B/ matches:
mcq.exp: \B requires NON-boundaries both sides — "cat" inside "scattered".

mcq.q: To match both candy and candies, the correct pattern is:
mcq.exp: Parentheses make the disjunction apply only to y|ies.

mcq.q: Which has the LOWEST precedence in a regular expression?
mcq.exp: Disjunction — which is exactly why the CAT|DOG example behaves as it does.

mcq.q: Which string is matched by /^CAT|DOG[0-9]*$/ but NOT by /^(CAT|DOG)[0-9]*$/?
mcq.exp: Without parentheses the | splits at the top level, so "starts with CAT" alone is enough.

mcq.q: In /the (.*)er they are, the \1er they will be/, the \1 refers to:

opts.t: the first character of the line
the text matched by the first parenthesised group

mcq.exp: \1 refers back to the text matched by group 1, not the pattern.

mcq.q: An FSA is defined by a tuple of how many components?
mcq.exp: Five: (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F).

mcq.q: In (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F), the symbol Σ represents:
mcq.exp: Σ is the alphabet.

mcq.q: The transition function signature is:
mcq.exp: δ: Q × Σ → Q.

mcq.q: In the sheep-talk FSA, δ("q3", "a") returns:
mcq.exp: q3 — the self-loop that gives "one or more a".

mcq.q: In the sheep-talk FSA, δ("q0", "a") returns:
mcq.exp: None — there is no transition on a from q0, so it is a failed state.

mcq.q: The regular expression for the sheep language is:
mcq.exp: /baa+!/ — b, then at least two a's, then !.

mcq.q: d_recognize("baaaa", machine) returns False because:

opts.t: b is not in the alphabet
there is no transition on a from q3
the tape ends in q3, which is not an accepting state

mcq.exp: The tape runs out in q3; only q4 is accepting. There is no "!".

mcq.q: A formal language is:

opts.t: a set of strings, each composed of symbols from a finite alphabet

mcq.exp: A set of strings over a finite alphabet.

mcq.q: L(m) denotes:

opts.t: the formal language characterized by the model m
the number of states in m

mcq.exp: "The formal language characterized by m".

mcq.q: In the English-numbers FSA, the set of accepting states is:
mcq.exp: Both q1 and q2 are double-circled.

mcq.q: In the English-numbers FSA, δ(q0, Tens) goes to:
mcq.exp: Tens takes you to q1; units and teens go straight to q2.

mcq.q: Why is ["one", "two"] rejected by the English-numbers FSA?

opts.t: the FSA only accepts two-word inputs
q2 is a dead/trap state for further input — units cannot follow units

mcq.exp: q2 is a dead/trap state — a unit cannot follow a unit.

mcq.q: What makes an FSA non-deterministic?

opts.t: it has more than three states
one (state, input) pair has more than one possible next state

mcq.exp: More than one possible next state for the same (state, input).

mcq.q: An ε-transition allows the machine to:

opts.t: move state without looking at the input or advancing the input pointer

mcq.exp: Move without consuming input.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the three standard solutions to non-determinism?
mcq.exp: The three are backup, look-ahead and parallelism.

mcq.q: The agenda in recognition-as-search operates as a:
mcq.exp: Last-In, First-Out.

mcq.q: In DFS, newly created states are added:

opts.t: to the back of the agenda
to the front of the agenda, so NEXT() selects the most recently created state first

mcq.exp: To the front, which is what makes the search depth-first.

mcq.q: In the CAT example, which path does NEXT() explore first?

opts.t: C → O → W, because it was added last and the stack is LIFO
C → A → T, because it was added first

mcq.exp: LIFO grabs the most recently pushed — the wrong path first, which is fine, it backtracks.

mcq.q: ND-RECOGNIZE-DFS returns ACCEPT when:

opts.t: the current state is in F, regardless of the tape
current_pos equals the input length AND current_q is in F
the tape is exhausted, regardless of state

mcq.exp: Both conditions are required — tape exhausted AND state in F.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a closure property of regular languages listed in the deck?
mcq.exp: The four are intersection, difference, complementation and reversal.

mcq.q: The class of regular languages is formally defined by which three operations?
mcq.exp: Concatenation, union and closure. The four closure properties (intersection, difference, complementation, reversal) are a separate list — do not confuse them.

mcq.q: Complementation of a regular language L₁ is written as:
mcq.exp: Σ* − L₁ — all possible strings not in L₁.

mcq.q: Which type of morphology produces a different form of the same base word without changing its part of speech?
mcq.exp: Inflectional — tense, number, case, without changing part of speech.

mcq.q: compute (verb) → computer (noun) → computational (adjective) is an example of:
mcq.exp: Derivational — the part of speech changes at each step.

mcq.q: Morphological parsing is implemented using:
mcq.exp: Finite-State Transducers — which is why morphology follows FSAs in the syllabus.

tf.q: Semantics deals with the speaker's intentions rather than literal meaning.

tf.exp: Correct as stated.

sa.q: Define NLP in one sentence.
sa.a: NLP provides computers with the capability of understanding text and spoken words in the same way a human being can understand, interpret and generate human language. Achieving this requires machines to hold much broader and deeper knowledge of language than simple keyword matching — six distinct levels of it.

sa.q: List the six levels of linguistic knowledge with a one-line definition each.
sa.a: Phonetics & Phonology — linguistic sounds. Morphology — the meaningful components of words. Syntax — the structural relationships between words. Semantics — meaning. Pragmatics — the relationship of meaning to the goals and intentions of the speaker. Discourse — linguistic units larger than a single utterance.

sa.q: Distinguish phonetics from phonology.
sa.a: Phonetics deals with the physical production of raw sounds; phonology deals with how our brain categorizes them into meaningful patterns. Example: the /p/ in "please" is released with a puff of air (aspiration) while the /p/ at the end of "cup" is not — phonetics describes that difference in production, phonology explains why English speakers still hear both as the same phoneme.

sa.q: Distinguish semantics from pragmatics using one example.
sa.a: Semantics is literal meaning regardless of context; pragmatics is how context, goals and intentions shape meaning. The deck uses one sentence for both: "I'm freezing." Semantically it means the speaker's body temperature has dropped to 0 °C. Pragmatically, said to a barista near an open door, it is an indirect request: "Could you please close the door?"

sa.q: What is discourse? Give the deck's example.
sa.a: Knowledge about linguistic units larger than a single utterance — conversations, paragraphs, narratives. The example is the four-turn exchange between Alex and Sam ("Hey, do you have a quick second?" / "Yeah, what's up?" / "Could you take a look at page 3 of this draft?" / "Sure, hand it over."). Discourse studies how individual sentences link into a cohesive dialogue, including turn-taking, context references and conversational flow.

sa.q: Apply any three levels of linguistic knowledge to HAL's line "I'm sorry, Dave, I'm afraid I can't do that."
sa.a: Morphology — "can't" is a contraction of the morphemes can + not. Syntax — a subordinate clause [I'm afraid] introducing an embedded main clause [I can't do that]. Pragmatics — HAL is not physically incapable of moving the doors; he is politely refusing to comply because he views Dave as a threat. (Also acceptable: Phonetics/Phonology — the calm monotone pitch and precise /d/ in "Dave"; Semantics — the literal expression of regret, fear and inability; Discourse — the multi-turn dialogue referencing their mutual conflict.)

sa.q: Define ambiguity and state its role in NLP.
sa.a: Ambiguity is multiple alternative linguistic structures arising from the same input. Its role: most tasks in speech and language processing can be viewed as resolving ambiguity, and it is the single biggest hurdle in NLP.

sa.q: Give the three types of ambiguity in "I saw the waiter with glasses", with a reading for each.
sa.a: Syntactic — "with glasses" attaches either to the noun "waiter" (a worker wearing spectacles) or to the verb "saw" (I used spectacles to spot him). Lexical/semantic — "glasses" means drinking tumblers, so the waiter was carrying serving glasses. Pragmatic — "with" means "in the physical company of", so the waiter was accompanied by drinking glasses: an odd image but grammatically valid.

sa.q: How is the ambiguity in "I made her duck" resolved?
sa.a: By using models to disambiguate. Whether duck is a verb or a noun is solved by part-of-speech tagging; whether make means "create" or "cook" is solved by word sense disambiguation. These are the two important kinds of lexical disambiguation.

sa.q: State Zipf's law and explain the long-tail problem.
sa.a: Frequency α 1 / Rank — a word's frequency is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table. The consequence is the long tail: rare occurrences collectively matter but are hard to train. Machines receive mountains of data for common words (is, a, the) but struggle to learn reliable representations for rare words.

sa.q: Why do sentences like "Will will will will's will?" defeat a parser?
sa.a: Because without understanding capitalization, context or part-of-speech tags, a computer cannot determine where the subject ends, where the action begins, and which "will" refers to a person versus an action or an object. The five tokens are: a person's name, the future-tense marker, the verb "to bequeath", a possessive naming a second person, and the noun for the legal document.

sa.q: Differentiate extractive and abstractive summarization.
sa.a: Extractive summarization pulls the most important sentences directly from a long document — the output is a subset of the input. Abstractive summarization generates a brand-new, concise overview — the output contains sentences that were never in the source.

sa.q: Differentiate text classification from topic modeling.
sa.a: Text classification automatically categorizes text into predefined labels (e.g. detecting phishing emails). Topic modeling discovers latent abstract themes across large document collections without human labeling. The distinction is whether the categories exist beforehand.

sa.q: Name and describe any three tasks from the Extraction table.
sa.a: Any three of: Invoice parsing — extracts structured financial data (amounts, dates, vendor names) from unstructured invoices. Key phrase extraction — pulls the most relevant and informative phrases from a document. NER — identifies and classifies proper nouns (persons, organizations, locations, dates). Medical NER — extracts clinical entities such as diseases, symptoms, medications and dosages. Event extraction — detects incidents and captures their participants, time, location and attributes. Relation mining — identifies semantic relationships between entities.

sa.q: Differentiate ASR, TTS and voice biometrics.
sa.a: ASR (speech-to-text) converts acoustic speech signals into written text — live captioning, voice dictation. TTS synthesizes written text into natural-sounding spoken audio with realistic intonation. Voice biometrics identifies or authenticates speakers from the unique phonetic characteristics of their voice. The first two are conversions in opposite directions; the third is an identification task.

sa.q: Reproduce the NLP pipeline, mapping each step to its unit.
sa.a: Step 1 Problem Definition & Context → Unit 1. Step 2 Signal Modality → Unit 2. Step 3 Data Preprocessing & Cleaning → Unit 3. Step 4 Linguistic Feature Extraction → Unit 5. Step 5 Language Modeling & Stats → Unit 4. Step 6 Deep Meaning & Context → Unit 6. Note that steps 4 and 5 map to units 5 then 4, crossing over.

sa.q: List the four stages of speech production with one line each.
sa.a: 1. Breathing — airflow serves as the source. 2. Phonation — action of the vocal folds in the larynx. 3. Resonance — the pharynx, oral and nasal cavity amplify the sound. 4. Articulation — the tongue, lips, teeth, palate and jaw shape and obstruct the airstream to produce distinct sounds.

sa.q: Differentiate voiced and unvoiced sounds with examples.
sa.a: Voiced sounds are made with the vocal folds together and vibrating — [b], [d], [g], [v], [z] and all the English vowels. Unvoiced (voiceless) sounds are made without this vocal cord vibration — [p], [t], [k], [f], [s].

sa.q: What are nasal sounds and which resonating cavities do they use?
sa.a: Most sounds are made by air passing through the mouth (oral cavity). Sounds made by air passing through the nose are nasal sounds, and they use both the oral and nasal tracts as resonating cavities. English nasal sounds are m, n and ng.

sa.q: Differentiate vowels, consonants and semivowels.
sa.a: Consonants are made by restricting or blocking the airflow and may be voiced or unvoiced. Vowels have less obstruction, are usually voiced, and are generally louder and longer-lasting. Semivowels have properties of both: voiced like vowels but short and less syllabic like consonants — [y] and [w].

sa.q: Differentiate place and manner of articulation.
sa.a: Place of articulation answers WHERE the constriction is — it is the point of maximum restriction. Manner of articulation answers HOW the restriction is made — complete blockage, turbulence, near-closure and so on.

sa.q: Explain stops, fricatives and affricates with examples.
sa.a: Stops (plosives) completely block airflow during the closure phase, followed by an explosive release — voiced [b], [d], [g] and unvoiced [p], [t], [k]. Fricatives constrict airflow to create turbulent "hissing" sounds — labiodentals [f, v], dentals [th, dh], alveolars [s, z], palato-alveolars [sh, zh]. Affricates combine a stop + fricative — [ch] as in "chicken", [jh] as in "giraffe".

sa.q: What are sibilants?
sa.a: The higher-pitched fricatives — [s], [z], [sh] and [zh].

sa.q: Why is /v/ classified differently from /w/?
sa.a: /v/ is a fricative — the articulators are close enough to create turbulent airflow. /w/ is an approximant — the articulators are close together but not narrow enough to create turbulence. The minimal pairs that show the contrast are Van/Wan, Vest/West, Vine/Wine.

sa.q: How are vowels classified, and what is a diphthong?
sa.a: Vowels are classified on two axes: tongue position (front and back) and height (high and low). A diphthong is a vowel in which the tongue position changes markedly during the production of the vowel.

sa.q: Compare IPA and ARPAbet on any three points.
sa.a: Scope: IPA is a universal system for all spoken human languages; ARPAbet is restricted to General American English. Symbols: IPA uses special Greek and Latin symbols, diacritics and modifiers ([ə], [æ], [ʃ], [θ]); ARPAbet uses 1- or 2-letter ASCII combinations (AX, AE, SH). Stress: IPA uses diacritic tick marks before stressed syllables (/ˈkæt/); ARPAbet uses numeric digits attached to vowel codes — 0 unstressed, 1 primary, 2 secondary (EH1).

sa.q: Define onset, nucleus, coda and rime.
sa.a: The nucleus is the vowel core of the syllable. The onset is the initial consonant or set of consonants (a complex onset when it is a cluster). The coda is the set of consonants following the nucleus. The rime (or rhyme) is the nucleus plus coda — the onset is not part of it.

sa.q: Segment "green" (/ɡriːn/) and "eggs" (/ɛɡz/) into onset, nucleus, coda and rime.
sa.a:
"green": onset /ɡr/ (a consonant cluster), nucleus /iː/, coda /n/ (a nasal consonant), rime /iːn/.
"eggs": onset empty — the syllable starts directly with a vowel; nucleus /ɛ/; coda /ɡz/ (a consonant cluster ending); rime /ɛɡz/.

sa.q: Why does "new" (/njuː/) have no rime?
sa.a: Because its coda is empty — it is an open syllable. Its onset is /nj/ (the /n/ followed by the palatal glide /j/) and its nucleus is /uː/, but with nothing after the nucleus there is no coda, and therefore no rime.

sa.q: Define prosody and name its three phenomena.
sa.a: Prosody is the acoustic and rhythmic properties of speech that extend over whole syllables, words or sentences rather than phonemes; it conveys how a phoneme is being spoken, adding nuance, emotion, structural boundaries and intent. Its three phenomena are intonation (sentence-level pitch contours), stress (lexical and contrastive) and syllable structure and phrasing (prosodic boundaries).

sa.q: Differentiate lexical and contrastive stress.
sa.a: Lexical stress distinguishes word meanings or parts of speech: "The manager certified his CONduct" (noun) vs "Teacher will conDUCT the exam" (verb). Contrastive stress highlights key information in a sentence: "I didn't take your book" (someone else took it) vs "I didn't take your book" (I took someone else's).

sa.q: Name the three acoustic parameters of prosody with their function.
sa.a: Fundamental frequency (pitch) — the rate of vocal fold vibration; expresses intonation, e.g. rising pitch for questions. Intensity / amplitude (loudness) — air pressure from the lungs; adds emphasis or stress. Duration (timing & rhythm) — speed and length of speech sounds; marks pauses, syllable elongation and overall tempo.

sa.q: Define sequence labelling and give one example.
sa.a: Sequence labelling is the task of assigning a categorical label to each item in a continuous sequence of input data, from raw acoustic signals to textual and semantic units. Example: voice activity detection, which labels each frame of an audio stream as speech or non-speech.

sa.q: What does a spectrogram show, and how is it written?
sa.a: A spectrogram shows how the frequency content of a signal varies with time. It is written as |X(m,k)| — the magnitude of Xm(ω) at ω = 2πk/N, where m is the time-frame index and k the frequency bin. The signal is sampled at fs = 1/T.

sa.q: List the four sources of noise in raw web text.
sa.a: HTML formatting, emojis, informal spellings and inconsistent casing. Raw text collected from the web or OCR is unstructured and noisy; the solution is a precise, rule-based formula to search, transform and clean text before feeding it to models or databases — i.e. regular expressions.

sa.q: Name and describe the four classes of OCR error.
sa.a: 1. Character-level swaps — visually similar characters are misidentified (0 vs O, 1 vs I/l, cl vs d, rn vs m). 2. Word boundary errors — missing or extra spaces ("UnitedStates"), hyper-segmentation ("I n f o r m a t i o n"), end-of-line hyphens ("proc- essing"). 3. Layout breakdown — multi-column text read straight across, table rows/columns flattened, headers/footers interrupting sentences. 4. Scan artifacts — dust and creases becoming mis-punctuation, currency signs and non-English symbols dropped or corrupted.

sa.q: Define a regular expression in two different ways.
sa.a: (1) A standard notation for characterizing text sequence — a mathematical and computational shorthand for describing a pattern of text, as +, *, −, / are for numerical expressions. (2) An algebraic notation for characterizing a set of strings: it uses special symbols to define a set of allowed texts (a language), and acts as the rulebook — any string that matches the pattern belongs to that language.

sa.q: Explain the difference between *, + and ?.
sa.a: * means zero or more of the preceding character — it therefore also matches the empty string. + means at least one. ? means the preceding character or nothing — i.e. zero or one. This is why an integer is /[0-9][0-9]*/ or /[0-9]+/ but not /[0-9]*/.

sa.q: Explain the difference between \b and \B using "The cat in the cathedral was scattered."
sa.a: \b matches a word boundary; \B matches a non-boundary. So /\bcat\b/ matches "cat" and rejects "cathedral" and "scattered", because those have no boundary on one or both sides. Conversely /\Bcat\B/ matches "scattered" (cat sits between two non-boundaries) and rejects "cat" and "cathedral".

sa.q: Write a regular expression to match the article "the", and explain each refinement.
sa.a:
/the/ — the naive version; it misses "The" because RE is case sensitive, and matches inside other words.
/[tT]he/ — the square-bracket disjunction now catches both cases, but it still matches inside other, theme and bathe.
/\b[tT]he\b/ — adding word boundaries restricts it to the standalone article. This is the correct answer.

sa.q: Explain substitution and backreferences in regular expressions.
sa.a:
Substitution: s/regexp1/pattern/ allows a string characterized by a regular expression to be replaced by another string — e.g. s/colour/color/.
Backreference: put parentheses around the first pattern and use the number operator \1 in the second pattern to refer back to it. /the (.*)er they are, the \1er they will be/ matches "The bigger they are, the bigger they will be". Crucially \1 matches the same text again, not merely the same pattern, so both halves must be identical.

sa.q: State the FSA 5-tuple and define each component.
sa.a: (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F). Q — the finite set of states, all possible conditions the system can be in. Σ — the alphabet, a finite set of input symbols accepted by the automaton. δ — the transition function, the rules dictating how the system moves from one state to another based on an input symbol (δ: Q × Σ → Q). q0 — the initial/start state, before any input is processed (q0 ∈ Q). F — the set of accepting/final states, where if processing ends the input is accepted (F ⊆ Q).
